claim: Over 90% of PDAC have oncogenic KRAS mutations.
source: Over 90% of PDAC have oncogenic KRAS mutations, and phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3Ks) are direct effectors of KRAS.
evidence: This is a statement of fact about PDAC genetics presented in the abstract without specific citation, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3Ks) are direct effectors of KRAS.
source: Over 90% of PDAC have oncogenic KRAS mutations, and phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3Ks) are direct effectors of KRAS.
evidence: This is a statement about the molecular relationship between KRAS and PI3Ks, presented as established knowledge.

claim: Ablation of Pik3ca in KPC pancreatic cancer cells induced host T cells to infiltrate and completely eliminate the tumors in a syngeneic orthotopic implantation mouse model.
source: Our previous study demonstrated that ablation of Pik3ca in KPC (KrasG12D; Trp53R172H; Pdx1-Cre) pancreatic cancer cells induced host T cells to infiltrate and completely eliminate the tumors in a syngeneic orthotopic implantation mouse model.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous study (Sivaram et al., 2019).

claim: Implantation of Pik3ca−/− KPC (αKO) cancer cells induces clonal enrichment of cytotoxic T cells infiltrating the pancreatic tumors.
source: Now, we show that implantation of Pik3ca−/− KPC (named αKO) cancer cells induces clonal enrichment of cytotoxic T cells infiltrating the pancreatic tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing and TCR repertoire analysis presented in Figure 1.

claim: Deletion of propionyl-CoA carboxylase subunit B gene (Pccb) in αKO cells leads to immune evasion, tumor progression, and death of host mice.
source: The result shows that deletion of propionyl-CoA carboxylase subunit B gene (Pccb) in αKO cells (named p-αKO) leads to immune evasion, tumor progression, and death of host mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the genome-wide CRISPR screen (Figure 2) and survival studies (Figure 3).

claim: p-αKO tumors are infiltrated with clonally enriched CD8+ T cells but they are inactive against tumor cells.
source: Surprisingly, p-αKO tumors are still infiltrated with clonally enriched CD8+ T cells but they are inactive against tumor cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data (Figure 4) and single-cell sequencing analysis (Figure 6).

claim: Blockade of PD-L1/PD1 interaction reactivated clonally enriched T cells infiltrating p-αKO tumors, leading to slower tumor progression and improved survival of host mice.
source: However, blockade of PD-L1/PD1 interaction reactivated these clonally enriched T cells infiltrating p-αKO tumors, leading to slower tumor progression and improve survival of host mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from PD1-null mice and anti-PD1 antibody treatment studies (Figure 5).

claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is expected to be the second leading cause of cancer death by 2030.
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most aggressive and lethal cancers, and it is expected to be the second leading cause of cancer death by 2030, with a 5-year survival rate of 12% (Siegel et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2023.

claim: PDAC has a 5-year survival rate of 12%.
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most aggressive and lethal cancers, and it is expected to be the second leading cause of cancer death by 2030, with a 5-year survival rate of 12% (Siegel et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2023.

claim: Most PDACs are classified as 'cold' tumors without infiltrating T cells and are resistant to currently available immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors.
source: Most PDACs are classified as 'cold' tumors without infiltrating T cells and are resistant to currently available immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors (Bian and Almhanna, 2021; Mucileanu et al., 2021; Balsano et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bian and Almhanna, 2021; Mucileanu et al., 2021; Balsano et al., 2023.

claim: A minority of PDAC patients have tumors that exhibit higher levels of infiltrating cytotoxic T cells and this observation is associated with longer survival.
source: However, a previous study showed that a minority of PDAC patients have tumors that already exhibit higher levels of infiltrating cytotoxic T cells and this observation is associated with longer survival of these patients (Balachandran et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Balachandran et al., 2017.

claim: G12D is the most common KRAS mutation (46%) in PDAC.
source: One of the most commonly dysregulated pathways in PDAC is oncogenic KRAS and G12D is the most common KRAS mutation (46%) in PDAC (Halbrook et al., 2023; Moore et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Halbrook et al., 2023 and Moore et al., 2020.

claim: PIK3CA isoform plays a critical role in the initiation of PDAC.
source: There are four PI3K catalytic isoforms and our group have previously shown that PIK3CA isoform plays a critical role in the initiation of PDAC (Wu et al., 2014) and mediates immune evasion once the tumors are formed (Sivaram et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2014.

claim: PIK3CA mediates immune evasion once PDAC tumors are formed.
source: There are four PI3K catalytic isoforms and our group have previously shown that PIK3CA isoform plays a critical role in the initiation of PDAC (Wu et al., 2014) and mediates immune evasion once the tumors are formed (Sivaram et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sivaram et al., 2019.

claim: KRAS signaling through PIK3CA can reduce the expression of MHC class I molecules, thus reducing antigen recognition and T-cell infiltration.
source: Our group reported that KRAS signaling through PIK3CA can reduce the expression of MHC class I molecules, thus reducing antigen recognition and T-cell infiltration (Sivaram et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sivaram et al., 2019.

claim: Genetic ablation of PIK3CA in KPC pancreatic tumor cells led to T-cell recognition and complete elimination by the host immune system in a syngeneic orthotopic implantation mouse model.
source: We showed that genetic ablation of PIK3CA in KPC (KrasG12D;Trp53R172H;Pdx1-Cre) pancreatic tumor cells led to T-cell recognition and complete elimination by the host immune system in a syngeneic orthotopic implantation mouse model (Sivaram et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sivaram et al., 2019.

claim: Analysis of CD8+ T cells' clonal size distribution revealed clonal enrichment in both αKO tumors, suggesting T cells in both tumors have been activated in response to tumor antigen.
source: Analysis of the CD8+ T cells' clonal size distribution revealed clonal enrichment in both αKO tumors, suggesting T cells in both tumors have been activated in response to tumor antigen (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Large clones are mapped to the Cd8_EffectorMem and Cd8_Tex, while non-clonal T cells mapped to the Naive/central memory T-cell group.
source: The degree of expansion observed among the clonotypes associated strongly with the phenotypic clusters of T cells, as large clones are mapped to the Cd8_EffectorMem and Cd8_Tex, while non-clonal T cells mapped to the Naive/centra memory T-cell group (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the UMAP visualization and TCR profiling data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: There is a massive expansion of Cd8_EffectorMem clones and these activated anti-tumor T cells are likely responsible for the immune-mediated elimination of αKO pancreatic tumors.
source: Taken together, these results show that there is a massive expansion of Cd8_EffectorMem clones and these activated anti-tumor T cells are likely are responsible for the immune-mediated elimination of αKO pancreatic tumors.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the single-cell sequencing data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The genome-scale CRISPR knockout (GeCKO v2) pooled lentiviral library A targets the complete mouse genome of 20,611 genes with three sgRNAs for each gene, as well as four sgRNAs for each of the 1175 miRNAs and 1000 control sgRNAs.
source: Briefly, αKO cells were first infected with the genome-scale CRISPR knockout (GeCKO v2) pooled lentiviral library A, which targets the complete mouse genome of 20,611 genes with three sgRNAs for each gene, as well as four sgRNAs for each of the 1175 miRNAs and 1000 control sgRNAs.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method and the composition of the GeCKO library used.

claim: Two out of eight mice 8 weeks after cell implantation exhibited tumor progression.
source: Indeed, two out of eight mice 8 weeks after cell implantation exhibited tumor progression, which were labeled as tumors #1 and #2 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by IVIS imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Four common sgRNA sequences were identified in both tumors targeting Pccb, Nr6a1, Ldoc1l, and Adck3.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, four common sgRNA sequences were identified in both tumors. The four targeted genes are Pccb (propionyl-CoA carboxylase), Nr6a1 (nuclear receptor subfamily 6 group A member 1), Ldoc1l (leucine-zipper protein 1), and Adck3 (aarF-domain-containing kinase 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by next-generation sequencing data from the CRISPR screen shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In both tumors, Pccb sgRNA sequence MGLibA ID 39695 was detected at many orders of magnitude higher than other three sgRNA sequences.
source: In both tumors, Pccb sgRNA sequence MGLibA ID 39695 was detected at many orders of magnitude higher than other three sgRNA sequences (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the NGS count data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC) has two subunits PCCA and PCCB and catalyzes the carboxylation of propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA, which is then converted to succinyl-CoA that enters the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA).
source: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC) has two subunits PCCA (propionyl-CoA carboxylase subunit A) and PCCB and catalyzes the carboxylation of propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA, which is then converted to succinyl-CoA that enters the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA).
evidence: This is a statement about the biochemical function of PCC, representing established knowledge.

claim: PCC dysfunction leads to a rare genetic disease called propionic acidemia.
source: PCC dysfunction leads to a rare genetic disease called propionic acidemia, which has been extensively studied (Wongkittichote et al., 2017; Shchelochkov et al., 1993; Grünert et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wongkittichote et al., 2017; Shchelochkov et al., 1993; Grünert et al., 2013.

claim: PCCB's role in cancer and whether it plays a role in the tumor immune response is completely unknown.
source: However, PCCB's role in cancer and whether it plays a role in the tumor immune response is completely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of prior knowledge regarding PCCB in cancer immunology.

claim: Most of the mice implanted with p-αKO cells exhibited tumor formation within 1 week.
source: Most of the mice exhibited tumor formation within 1 week.
evidence: This claim is supported by IVIS imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In all the animals implanted with p-αKO cells, pancreatic tumors eventually progressed and 9 out of 12 mice died by week #8.
source: However, in all the animals, pancreatic tumors eventually progressed and 9 out of 12 mice died by week #8 when the experiment was stopped (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: 100% of mice implanted with KPC cells died by week #3.
source: In comparison, while 100% of mice implanted with KPC cells died by week #3, all mice implanted with αKO cells remained tumor free by week #8 (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All mice implanted with αKO cells remained tumor free by week #8.
source: In comparison, while 100% of mice implanted with KPC cells died by week #3, all mice implanted with αKO cells remained tumor free by week #8 (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: PCCB loss can reverse immune recognition of αKO cells.
source: These results indicate that PCCB loss can reverse immune recognition of αKO cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the survival and tumor progression data comparing αKO and p-αKO cells.

claim: p-αKO cells grew at a similar rate compared to αKO cells in standard 2D culture.
source: In standard 2D culture, p-αKO cells grew at a similar rate compared to αKO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both αKO and p-αKO cell lines exhibited significantly slower growth rate than KPC cells.
source: Note that both αKO and p-αKO cell lines exhibited significantly slower growth rate than KPC cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The reduced growth rate of αKO and p-αKO cells explains, at least in part, the longer survival time of p-αKO implanted mice compared with KPC-implanted mice.
source: This reduced growth rate explains, at least in part, the longer survival time of p-αKO implanted mice compared with KPC-implanted mice, where the median survival of KPC was 15.5 days and the median survival of p-αKO 40.5 days (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the growth rate and survival data.

claim: The loss of PCCB did not reverse the changes in PIK3CA–AKT signaling in αKO cells.
source: In summary, the loss of PCCB did not reverse the changes in PIK3CA–AKT signaling in αKO cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Progression of p-αKO tumors is through a pathway independent of PI3K and AKT.
source: These results indicate that progression of p-αKO tumors is through a pathway independent of PI3K and AKT.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the western blotting data showing no changes in PI3K-AKT signaling.

claim: The mitochondrial function and intracellular glycolysis and TCA metabolite changes showed comparable levels between αKO and p-αKO cell lines.
source: In addition, the mitochondrial function evaluated by measuring the oxygen consumption rate (OCR) with Seahorse, as well as the intracellular glycolysis and TCA metabolite changes measured by untargeted liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS) both showed comparable levels between αKO and p-αKO cell lines, indicating that the increased growth of p-αKO cells in vivo is probably not due to PCCB-related mitochondrial metabolic changes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse OCR data and LC-MS metabolite analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and 1E.

claim: The increased growth of p-αKO cells in vivo is probably not due to PCCB-related mitochondrial metabolic changes.
source: In addition, the mitochondrial function evaluated by measuring the oxygen consumption rate (OCR) with Seahorse, as well as the intracellular glycolysis and TCA metabolite changes measured by untargeted liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS) both showed comparable levels between αKO and p-αKO cell lines, indicating that the increased growth of p-αKO cells in vivo is probably not due to PCCB-related mitochondrial metabolic changes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, E).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the metabolic analysis data.

claim: p-αKO tumors were highly infiltrated with T cells, similar to αKO tumors.
source: Unexpectedly, p-αKO tumors were also highly infiltrated with T cells, similar to αKO tumors, and as expected, KPC tumors were mostly devoid of T cells (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: KPC tumors were mostly devoid of T cells.
source: Unexpectedly, p-αKO tumors were also highly infiltrated with T cells, similar to αKO tumors, and as expected, KPC tumors were mostly devoid of T cells (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: The conversion of cold KPC tumor into inflamed αKO tumor upon genetic deletion of Pik3ca in KPC was not reversed by ablation of PCCB.
source: Therefore, the conversion of cold KPC tumor into inflamed αKO tumor upon genetic deletion of Pik3ca in KPC was not reversed by ablation of PCCB.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the immunohistochemistry data showing T cell infiltration in p-αKO tumors.

claim: p-αKO tumors displayed markedly elevated cell counts positive for PD1, CTLA4, and LAG3 compared to αKO tumor sections.
source: In contrast to αKO tumor sections, p-αKO tumors displayed markedly elevated cell counts positive for PD1, CTLA4, and LAG3.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Infiltrating CD8+ T cells in p-αKO tumors might be functionally exhausted with compromised anti-tumor cytotoxic activity.
source: These results suggest that infiltrating CD8+ T cells in p-αKO tumors might be functionally exhausted with compromised anti-tumor cytotoxic activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the elevated expression of checkpoint inhibitory receptors.

claim: There is a significant twofold increase in M2 macrophage infiltration within the p-αKO tumors.
source: The results revealed a significant twofold increase in M2 macrophage infiltration within the p-αKO tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: After 8 weeks, eight out of nine PD1-null mice implanted with p-αKO cells were still alive and five of the animals were tumor free.
source: After 8 weeks when the experiment ended, eight out nine mice were still alive and five of the animals were tumor free (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival and IVIS imaging data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: After 8 weeks of anti-PD1 treatment, 9 out of 13 anti-PD1-treated mice were alive whereas only 2 out of 9 vehicle-treated mice survived.
source: After 8 weeks of treatment, 9 out 13 anti-PD1-treated mice were alive whereas only 2 out 9 vehicle-treated mice survived (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Four mice in the anti-PD1-treated group remained tumor free.
source: Four mice in the anti-PD1-treated group remained tumor free.
evidence: This claim is supported by IVIS imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: All vehicle-treated mice developed large pancreatic tumors including the two surviving mice at week #8.
source: In contrast, all vehicle-treated mice developed large pancreatic tumors including the two surviving mice at week #8 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by IVIS imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There is large clonal enrichment of CD8+ T cells in p-αKO tumors implanted in either WT or PD1-null mice.
source: Similar to what we observed in αKO tumors (see Figure 1), there is large clonal enrichment of CD8+ T cells in p-αKO tumors implanted in either WT or PD1-null mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The number of clonotypes with large expansions is much higher in tumors implanted in PD1-null mice.
source: Interestingly, the number of clonotypes with large expansions is much higher in tumors implanted in PD1-null mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The number of clonotypes observed in p-αKO tumors implanted in PD1-null mice is even greater than those found in αKO tumors implanted in WT mice.
source: Indeed, the number of clonotypes observed in p-αKO tumors implanted in PD1-null mice is even greater than those found in αKO tumors implanted in WT mice.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of TCR sequencing data between different experimental groups.

claim: Large expansion clonotypes mainly mapped to EffectorMem and Tex gene expression profiles in both WT and PD1-null mice.
source: Again, in both groups, large expansion clonotypes mainly mapped to EffectorMem and Tex gene expression profiles.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There are many more CD8+ clonotypes that mapped to the EffectorMem in tumors implanted in PD1-null mice as compared to WT mice.
source: There are many more CD8+ clonotypes that mapped to the EffectorMem in tumors implanted in PD1-null mice as compared to WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: 856 CD8+ T cells (all 18 large expansion clonotypes) were observed in the EffectorMem group for tumors implanted in PD1-null mice, whereas only 361 cells (from 3 clones) appeared in tumors implanted in WT mice.
source: Notably, 856 CD8+ T cells (all 18 large expansion clonotypes) were observed in the EffectorMem group for tumors implanted in PD1-null mice, whereas only 361 cells (from 3 clones) were observed appeared in tumors implanted in WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: More CD8+ EffectorMem cells were found in p-αKO tumors implanted in PD1-null mice than αKO tumors implanted in WT mice (856 vs. 559).
source: Indeed, we found more CD8+ EffectorMem cells in p-αKO tumors implanted in PD1-null mice then αKO tumors implanted in WT mice (856 vs. 559).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: Regression of p-αKO tumors implanted in mice with PD1/PD-L1 blockade is due to reactivation of anti-tumor cytotoxic T cells.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that regression of p-αKO tumors implanted in mice with PD1/PD-L1 blockade is due to reactivation of anti-tumor cytotoxic T cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the single-cell sequencing data showing increased effector memory T cells.

claim: Immune checkpoint blockade, such as anti-PD1, promotes Tpex to generate effector T cells.
source: Recent studies propose that immune checkpoint blockade, such as anti-PD1, promotes Tpex to generate effector T cells (Kallies et al., 2020; Im et al., 2016; Utzschneider et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kallies et al., 2020; Im et al., 2016; Utzschneider et al., 2016.

claim: p-αKO tumors implanted in WT mice exhibit a distinct population of Tpex that transform into effector memory T cells upon treatment with anti-PD1 antibody.
source: Our findings are consistent with this hypothesis, p-αKO tumors implanted in WT mice exhibit a distinct population of Tpex. Treatment with an anti-PD1 antibody resulted in their transformation into effector memory T cells, as observed in p-αKO tumors implanted in the PD1-null mice.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the single-cell sequencing data comparing WT and PD1-null mice.

claim: Patients with higher PCCB/PIK3CA ratio trended to have better survival compared with patients with lower PCCB/PIK3CA ratio.
source: Compared with patients with lower PCCB/PIK3CA ratio, patients with higher ratio trended to have better survival (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of TCGA database shown in Figure 7A.

claim: PCCB expression is significantly lower in tumor sections compared with adjacent normal tissues in PDAC patients.
source: Both data revealed significantly lower PCCB expressions in tumor sections compared with adjacent normal tissues (Figure 7B), which is consistent with our observation that low PCCB levels lead to tumor progression.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of GEO datasets GSE15471 and GSE16515 shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Among PDAC patients with high CD8+ infiltrating T cells, patients with high PCCB showed survival benefits over patients with low PCCB expression.
source: Among the PDAC patients with high CD8+ infiltrating T cells (TCGA PDAC database), patients with high PCCB showed survival benefits over patients with low PCCB expression, which again indicates the T-cell-mediated survival benefits of PCCB expression in PDAC patients (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of TCGA database shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The PI3K signaling pathway plays an important role in regulating the immune microenvironment in PDAC.
source: The PI3K signaling pathway plays an important role in regulating the immune microenvironment in PDAC, and previous studies have indicated that specific PIK3CA inhibitors hold promise in transforming immune-deficient cold tumors into inflamed, hot tumors (Sun et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2016; Liu and Sun, 2021; Borcoman et al., 2019; Sai et al., 2017; Sun and Meng, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Specific PIK3CA inhibitors hold promise in transforming immune-deficient cold tumors into inflamed, hot tumors.
source: The PI3K signaling pathway plays an important role in regulating the immune microenvironment in PDAC, and previous studies have indicated that specific PIK3CA inhibitors hold promise in transforming immune-deficient cold tumors into inflamed, hot tumors (Sun et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2016; Liu and Sun, 2021; Borcoman et al., 2019; Sai et al., 2017; Sun and Meng, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sun et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2016; Liu and Sun, 2021; Borcoman et al., 2019; Sai et al., 2017; Sun and Meng, 2020.

claim: Downregulation of PIK3CA in tumor cells enhances their recognition and elimination by T cells.
source: Our previous investigations with a PDAC mouse model revealed that downregulation of PIK3CA in tumor cells enhances their recognition and elimination by T cells (Sivaram et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sivaram et al., 2019.

claim: Deleting PCCB in pancreatic tumor cells lacking PIK3CA leads to immune evasion, tumor progression, and ultimately, the death of the host animal.
source: Notably, we discovered that the loss of PCCB, a subunit of the mitochondrial enzyme propionyl-CoA carboxylase, can entirely reverse the immune recognition phenotype resulting from PIK3CA downregulation. Deleting PCCB in pancreatic tumor cells lacking PIK3CA leads to immune evasion, tumor progression, and ultimately, the death of the host animal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the CRISPR screen and survival studies.

claim: Implanting p-αKO cells into PD1-null mice significantly improved mouse survival.
source: Intriguingly, implanting p-αKO cells into PD1-null mice significantly improved mouse survival, hinting at the partial attribution of immune evasion in p-αKO tumors to elevated PD1 expression on T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Treatment of p-αKO tumors with an anti-PD1 neutralizing antibody yielded comparable results to implanting p-αKO cells in PD1-null mice.
source: Furthermore, treatment of p-αKO tumors with an anti-PD1 neutralizing antibody yielded comparable results, highlighting the potential applicability of this approach in PDAC treatment, especially when coupled with a PIK3CA inhibitor.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Blocking the PD-L1/PD1 interaction results in T-cell-mediated elimination of p-αKO tumor cells.
source: Noteworthy outcomes ensued when interfering with the PD-L1/PD1 axis, resulting in T-cell-mediated elimination of p-αKO tumor cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival and imaging data from PD1 blockade experiments.

claim: Single-cell sequencing substantiates that blocking the PD-L1/PD1 interaction reactivates clonal anti-tumor T cells.
source: Single-cell sequencing substantiates these findings by confirming that blocking the PD-L1/PD1 interaction reactivates clonal anti-tumor T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Improved anti-tumor effects were observed in melanoma and fibrosarcoma models upon the combination of PI3K inhibitors with PD-1 blockade.
source: In a study by Isoyama et al., 2021, improved anti-tumor effects were observed in melanoma and fibrosarcoma models upon the combination of PI3K inhibitors with PD-1 blockade.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Isoyama et al., 2021.

claim: PIK3CA was identified as a factor promoting resistance to anti-PD1 treatment in a colon carcinoma model.
source: Similarly, Collins et al., 2022 conducted an in vivo expression screen with a pool of known oncogenes and identified PIK3CA as a factor promoting resistance to anti-PD1 treatment in a colon carcinoma model.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Collins et al., 2022.

claim: The resistance to immunotherapy was successfully overturned with the administration of a PI3K inhibitor.
source: Notably, the resistance to immunotherapy was successfully overturned with the administration of a PI3K inhibitor.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Collins et al., 2022.

claim: The administration of anti-PD1 neutralizing antibody did not achieve 100% efficacy.
source: Although the administration of anti-PD1 neutralizing antibody yielded promising results, the treatment alone did not achieve 100% efficacy.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data showing some mice still died despite treatment.

claim: Not all exhausted T cells were reactivated in PD1-null mice, potentially explaining why some of the mice still succumb to tumor progression despite PD-L1/PD1 blockade.
source: Indeed, our scRNA-seq result from PD1-null mice revealed that not all exhausted T cells were reactivated, potentially explaining why some of the mice still succumb to tumor progression despite PD-L1-/PD1 blockade.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from single-cell sequencing data.

claim: LAG3, although demonstrating limited efficacy as a monotherapy, is frequently used in combination with other checkpoint inhibitors.
source: LAG3, although demonstrating limited efficacy as a monotherapy, is frequently used in combination with other checkpoint inhibitors (Gulhati et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gulhati et al., 2023.

claim: The dual blockade of PD-1 and TIGIT has demonstrated superior clinical benefits in cancer treatment.
source: Similarly, while anti-TIGIT antibodies have shown remarkable effectiveness in treating solid tumors, the dual blockade of PD-1 and TIGIT has demonstrated superior clinical benefits in cancer treatment (Smith et al., 2013; Tedelind et al., 2007; Høgh et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2013; Tedelind et al., 2007; Høgh et al., 2020.

claim: There is a significant upregulation of both TIGIT and LAG3 in p-αKO tumors.
source: Our IHC data notably revealed a significant upregulation of both TIGIT and LAG3 in p-αKO tumors, suggesting that the inclusion of additional immune checkpoint inhibitors, alongside PD1 inhibition, may further improve treatment outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Propionic acidemia is caused by mutations in Pccb or Pcca subunits, which impair PCC function.
source: Previous studies primarily focused on the role of Pccb in the genetic disease propionic acidemia, caused by mutations in Pccb or Pcca subunits, which impair PCC function (Wongkittichote et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wongkittichote et al., 2017.

claim: Dysfunctional PCC leads to the accumulation of propionyl-CoA and other byproducts such as propionylcarnitine (C3), methylcitrate (MC), and 3-hydroxypropionate (3OHPA).
source: Dysfunctional PCC leads to the accumulation of propionyl-CoA and other byproducts such as propionylcarnitine (C3), methylcitrate (MC), and 3-hydroxypropionate (3OHPA) (Kurczynski et al., 1989; Ando et al., 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kurczynski et al., 1989; Ando et al., 1972.

claim: Intracellular metabolite analysis by LC–MS showed elevated MC and C3 levels upon Pccb deletion, although the statistical significance was not reached.
source: Intracellular metabolite analysis by LC–MS showed elevated MC and C3 levels upon Pccb deletion, although the statistical significance was not reach (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Intracellular propionyl-CoA levels were similar between αKO and p-αKO cells.
source: Importantly, intracellular propionyl-CoA levels were similar between αKO and p-αKO cells, potentially due to its conversion to MC and C3.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Propionic acid regulates colonic Treg (cTreg) homeostasis in the gut lumen.
source: Smith et al., 2013 demonstrated that propionic acid regulates colonic Treg (cTreg) homeostasis in the gut lumen.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Smith et al., 2013.

claim: Propionic acid supplementation in the drinking water of germ-free (GF) mice increased cTreg frequency and number in the gut lumen.
source: Propionic acid supplementation in the drinking water of germ-free (GF) mice increased cTreg frequency and number in the gut lumen, while Tregs in the spleen, mesenteric lymph nodes, and thymus remained unaffected.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Smith et al., 2013.

claim: Treatment of cTregs isolated from GF mice with propionate led to increased Foxp3 and IL10 expressions.
source: Treatment of cTregs isolated from GF mice with propionate led to increased Foxp3 and IL10 expressions, both of which play important roles in Treg-mediated immune suppression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Smith et al., 2013.

claim: Propionate suppressed the secretion of TNFα and IL8 from neutrophils, inhibited the NF-κB pathway, and downregulated immune-related genes in a colon cell line.
source: Another study by Tedelind et al., 2007 reported that propionate suppressed the secretion of TNFα and IL8 from neutrophils, inhibited the NF-κB pathway, and downregulated immune-related genes in a colon cell line (Tedelind et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tedelind et al., 2007.

claim: Propionate upregulated the surface expression of the immune stimulatory NKG2D ligands MHC-class-I-related family (MICA/B) on several cancer cells and activated T cells, mediated by mTORC2.
source: Recently, Hogh et al. reported that propionate upregulated the surface expression of the immune stimulatory NKG2D ligands MHC-class-I-related family (MICA/B) on several cancer cells and activated T cells, mediated by mTORC2 (Høgh et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Høgh et al., 2020.

claim: RNA sequencing of αKO and p-αKO cells revealed substantial changes in several cytokine-related signaling pathways.
source: RNA sequencing of αKO and p-αKO cells revealed substantial changes in several cytokine-related signaling pathways, indicating potential cytokine involvement in regulating PD1 expression on T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: This study is the first to report an association between PCCB and PIK3CA.
source: Our study is the first to report an association between PCCB and PIK3CA.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings in this study.

claim: PIK3CA knockout cells (αKO) were used instead of conventional PIK3CA inhibitors to avoid off-target effects.
source: We utilized PIK3CA knockout cells (αKO) instead of conventional PIK3CA inhibitors to avoid off-target effects reported in previous studies (Wang et al., 2017; Gharbi et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2019; Kong and Yamori, 2008), providing a more specific and accurate assessment of PIK3CA's role in regulating immune responses in PDAC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies reporting off-target effects of PIK3CA inhibitors.

claim: PCCB regulates immune evasion by promoting increased PD-L1 expression in anti-tumor cytotoxic T cells.
source: We showed that PCCB regulates immune evasion by promoting increased PD-L1 expression in anti-tumor cytotoxic T cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the immunohistochemistry and functional data.

claim: The resistance of PDAC to PI3K inhibitors and checkpoint inhibitors could potentially be surmounted by deploying both drugs in combination.
source: Consequently, our findings suggest that the resistance of PDAC to PI3K inhibitors and checkpoint inhibitors could potentially be surmounted by deploying both drugs in combination.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation from the experimental findings.
